## Findings

### F1. High: Analytics disclosure does not match the full data flow

The version of `webpage/privacy-policy.html` on `main` called analytics anonymous and said it did not collect location. This draft replaces those claims. The PostHog SDK creates a persistent pseudonymous identifier and attaches app, device, operating-system, locale, time-zone, and screen details. The app sends `location_used` and `has_location` events, but it does not send GPS coordinates or place labels as event fields. The SDK also exposes the request IP to PostHog. Its IP-based location estimate is not disabled in app configuration. [Current policy draft](../webpage/privacy-policy.html), [PostHog setup](../src/config/posthog.ts#L3-L23), [locked SDK version](../pnpm-lock.yaml#L2321-L2332), [location event](../src/services/location/useLocation.ts#L30-L40), and [entry events](../src/screens/compose/Compose.tsx#L213-L224).

The app has no analytics opt-out. The privacy screen contains app lock, backup, and storage controls only. The production token is not in the repository. EAS selects a remote `production` environment, so this review cannot confirm whether production analytics are active. [Privacy screen](../src/screens/settings/PrivacySettings.tsx#L389-L464), [EAS profile](../eas.json#L7-L25), [environment template](../.env.example#L1), and [development guide](../DEVELOPMENT.md#L15-L18).

### F2. High: Error reports and launch URLs are not fully scrubbed

The app enables capture of unhandled JavaScript errors and rejected promises. `PostHogErrorBoundary` also sends error details and a component stack. Manual reports replace file paths with `<path>`, but automatic reports do not use that helper. The PostHog lifecycle event can also include the app launch URL. No global filter or launch-URL scrubber appears in the app configuration. No content leak was confirmed, but an exception message or URL can contain personal information. [PostHog setup](../src/config/posthog.ts#L11-L19), [error boundary](../App.tsx#L121-L129), [app scheme](../app.json#L5-L12), [locked SDK version](../pnpm-lock.yaml#L2321-L2332), and [manual error reporting](../src/shared/utils/devLog.ts#L11-L39).

### F3. High: Local storage, backups, and app lock need clearer limits

The app uses SQLite and app files without an application-level encryption layer. The app lock calls the device authentication prompt, but it does not encrypt entries or attachments. The source also notes that the operating system can take an app-switcher snapshot before the JavaScript cover appears. [Database](../src/services/db/database.ts#L1-L28), [app lock](../src/services/auth/useAppLock.ts#L22-L47), and [lock storage](../src/services/auth/appLockStore.ts#L30-L56).

The manual `.openlog` archive is not encrypted. A copy can remain in app cache if saving or sharing fails after export. Android system backup includes shared preferences, but the repository does not list every value that libraries can store there. iOS app data has no configured backup exclusion. The current policy did not explain these paths. [Export archive](../src/services/backup/export/index.ts#L125-L132), [export cleanup](../src/services/backup/export/index.ts#L320-L324), [share fallback](../src/screens/settings/PrivacySettings.tsx#L137-L171), and [backup rules](../plugins/withAndroidBackupRules.js#L12-L38).

### F4. Medium: Location, font, website, and contact requests need disclosure

A location action sends coordinates to the native geocoder. iOS uses Core Location. Android calls the Android Geocoder API, but the repository does not name its downstream provider. The policy did not describe this request. The existing review file already lists this gap as P3-5. [Location service](../src/services/location/location.ts#L63-L85) and [open review finding](./review-findings.md#L9-L17).

The app also requests optional fonts from jsDelivr. The website stylesheet requests Google Fonts, and GitHub Pages hosts the site. A person who emails the listed Gmail address sends their message and any attached files to that mailbox. The code does not define retention for website logs or email. [Font resolver](../src/services/fonts/resolver.ts#L16-L27), [site CSS](../webpage/style.css#L1), [Pages workflow](../.github/workflows/pages.yml#L17-L36), and [contact address](../webpage/index.html#L15-L21).

### F5. Medium: Permission timing and attachment metadata need review

The app requests notification permission shortly after the timeline opens, not when a person starts a backup. Local completion notifications can show entry counts and backup size. The iOS configuration declares photo-library write use, but the reviewed app code opens a share sheet and does not call a photo-library write API. The image path can keep the original file, so embedded metadata can remain. [Timeline prompt](../src/screens/timeline/Timeline.tsx#L17-L39), [notification content](../src/services/notifications/notifications.ts#L65-L94), [iOS permission string](../app.json#L14-L25), [image path](../src/services/media/images.ts#L11-L48), and [share action](../src/services/media/share.ts#L15-L32).

The attachment picker accepts any file type. It can open selected files in another app. The policy did not describe file-provider or share-target handling. [Document picker](../src/services/media/attachments.ts#L20-L68).

The privacy contact uses a Gmail address. The code does not define mailbox-provider retention or how the owner handles requests. [Contact address](../webpage/index.html#L15-L21).

### F6. Medium: Public claims are broader than the implementation

The README says content stays on the device and is never uploaded. The website says the app works offline. The About screen says everything stays on the device. The terms say local content is not uploaded or synced. These statements omit PostHog telemetry, geocoding, font requests, system backups, and user-selected sharing. The old policy also promised practical notice for material changes, but no in-app notice path appears in the app. [README](../README.md#L7-L15), [website](../webpage/index.html#L85-L102), [About screen](../src/screens/settings/AboutSettings.tsx#L79-L84), and [terms](../webpage/terms.html#L27-L38).

The product guide says analytics never include locations. The app sends location-use and location-presence events. These events do not contain exact coordinates, so the guide and event design need a shared definition of location data. [Product guide](../AGENTS.md#L13-L16), [location event](../src/services/location/useLocation.ts#L30-L40), and [entry event fields](../src/screens/compose/Compose.tsx#L213-L224).

### F7. Medium: Retention, rights, operator, age, and jurisdiction are unknown

The app sets no local content expiry and has no single control that clears entries, profile details, preferences, font files, and analytics state. Delete-all removes entries, tags, drafts, and unreferenced media, but leaves profile and app preferences. SQLite deletion does not promise secure erasure. PostHog retention, website log retention, and email retention are not defined in the repository. [Delete-all action](../src/modules/entry/store/EntryStore.ts#L139-L147), [privacy settings](../src/screens/settings/PrivacySettings.tsx#L375-L386), and [database setup](../src/services/db/schema.ts#L33-L50).

The previous policy said OpenLog is not directed to children under 13, but the app does not ask for age or enforce an age limit. The repository names Rwitesh Bera as maker but does not give a legal operator name, postal address, target countries, or privacy-request process. It also does not contain Google Play Data Safety or Apple App Privacy disclosures. [Policy draft](../webpage/privacy-policy.html), [public contact and terms](../webpage/terms.html#L63-L79), [Android release workflow](../.github/workflows/release-android.yml#L1-L20), and [iOS config](../app.json#L11-L25).

## Recommendations

1. Confirm the production PostHog token, data region, GeoIP behavior, retention, processor terms, subprocessors, and deletion process.
2. Add a user-facing analytics choice or confirm that analytics run by default. Update the policy and store disclosures to match.
3. Disable launch-URL capture unless the app needs it. Add a tested event scrubber for exception text, stack traces, paths, and query values.
4. Decide whether to add encryption for local content and backup archives. Document Android and iOS system-backup behavior. Remove temporary export files on every exit path.
5. Confirm the Android geocoder provider. Keep location use explicit and document that the platform geocoder receives coordinates.
6. Remove the unused photo-library write permission or add and document the feature that needs it. Use the narrowest photo-picker access available. Remove photo metadata before storage or explain that it can remain.
7. Move the notification prompt to a backup action. Limit completion details that appear on lock screens.
8. Self-host website fonts or disclose Google Fonts requests. Document GitHub Pages and contact-mail retention.
9. Align the README, website, About screen, terms, and product guide with the confirmed data flows.
10. Define retention, deletion, and privacy-request steps. Confirm the legal operator, address, age range, user countries, supported platforms, and notice process before publication.

## Owner clarifications

1. Does the production EAS environment contain `EXPO_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN`? Which release builds send PostHog events?
2. What PostHog region, retention period, GeoIP configuration, data-processing terms, and subprocessor list apply? Who handles deletion requests?
3. Does the owner want automatic error and launch-URL capture? What legal basis and user choice apply to analytics and location requests in each market?
4. Who is the legal operator and data controller? What legal name, postal address, privacy contact, and email-retention period belong in the policy?
5. Which countries and age groups does OpenLog serve? Is the iOS configuration a released product, and is any web app available?
6. What data can Android shared preferences contain? Does the owner intend Android cloud backup and device transfer? Does the owner want iOS backups to include app data?
7. Which service resolves Android coordinates? What service terms and retention apply to coordinates sent by the platform geocoder?
8. Does any supported feature save photos directly to the photo library? What rules apply to attachment metadata and files selected from cloud providers?
9. What privacy-request process and notice process does the owner use? Does any business practice share or sell data beyond the flows in this repository?

## Regulatory review

The repository does not establish the country of the operator, user countries, age range, or business thresholds. This review cannot decide which laws apply. Counsel must assess the launch markets. Candidate laws include GDPR, UK GDPR, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of India, US state privacy laws, and COPPA. Counsel must assess COPPA if the service targets children or the owner knows a child under 13 uses it.

Use data minimization, purpose limits, retention limits, and privacy by design as review criteria. Confirm Google Play Data Safety and Apple App Privacy disclosures against the final build. This code review does not establish compliance with any law or security standard.

• Recording duration, backup entry count, and backup file size.
  • Location use, app-lock changes, and the notification permission choice.

    • These event fields do not include entry text, media files, attachment names, or exact location coordinates. The app sends a persistent installation ID that does not contain your name. PostHog can use this ID to link events from the same installation. The SDK stores the ID and pending events in app storage. The app does not set an expiry for the event queue. The app does not add your profile name or email address to product-event fields.

    The PostHog SDK also sends the app identifier, version, build, and environment. It sends device model and manufacturer, operating system and version, locale, time zone, and screen size. PostHog receives the network request IP address. The app leaves PostHog's IP-based location estimate on. PostHog can infer an approximate region from that address, subject to project configuration. Events go to PostHog's US endpoint. OpenLog uses these events for product analytics and error diagnosis.

    An app-open event can include the launch URL supplied by the operating system. The SDK also captures unhandled JavaScript errors, rejected promises, and errors from an app error boundary. Error reports can include error messages and stack traces. The app redacts file paths from errors sent through its manual reporting helper. Automatic error reports do not use that helper. An error message or launch URL can contain personal information.

    The app does not record session replay, capture taps automatically, or collect console logs. The code does not set a PostHog data-retention period. PostHog's privacy policy and project settings govern its handling and retention.

    Location

    OpenLog requests foreground location only when you ask to add or refresh a place. It sends the coordinates to the native geocoding service to get a place label. iOS uses Apple's Core Location geocoder. Android uses the Android Geocoder API. The code does not name a fixed downstream provider for Android. These services can receive your coordinates.

    OpenLog saves the coordinates and returned place label in the draft or entry on your device. It does not track location in the background. Analytics record whether you used location, not the coordinates or place label.

    Fonts and the website

    If you select an optional font that is not cached, OpenLog downloads it from the jsDelivr CDN and stores it on your device. The request identifies the font file and sends ordinary network data, such as your IP address. It does not include entry content. The app keeps downloaded fonts until you remove them or the operating system removes app data.

    GitHub Pages hosts the OpenLog website. The website stylesheet requests fonts from Google Fonts. GitHub and Google receive website and font requests with ordinary connection data. The native app does not use browser cookies. The website source contains no analytics script or cookie code. The repository does not show the hosting providers' log or cookie practices. Read the GitHub privacy statement and Google Privacy Policy.

    The website links to external services. If you open one, that service handles your visit under its own privacy terms.

    Permissions and notifications

    OpenLog uses these device permissions and pickers:

    • Photo-library access when you choose images to attach.
    • Microphone access when you start a recording.
    • Foreground location access when you ask to add or refresh a place.
    • The system file picker when you choose an attachment or backup.

    OpenLog asks for notification permission shortly after the timeline opens. If you allow it, the app creates local notifications for backup and import progress. A completion notice can show the entry count and backup file size. The device can show these notices on its lock screen, subject to your notification settings. The code does not register a remote push-notification token.

    Backups and sharing

    When you export a backup, OpenLog creates a compressed archive with your entries, tags, app settings, profile name, locations, attachment details, and media files. OpenLog does not encrypt this archive. The app first writes it to temporary storage, then saves it to a folder you choose or opens the system share sheet. A file provider or app that you choose can receive a copy. OpenLog does not receive the copy that you save outside the app.

    When you share a photo or open an attachment in another app, that app can receive the selected file. The device file picker can also show files from cloud storage providers. Those providers handle the file under their own terms.

    Android system backup is enabled. OpenLog's Android rules include shared-preference files and exclude the SQLite database, media, drafts, and SecureStore preferences. Android can copy included preferences to its configured backup or device-transfer service. The code does not identify every value that another library can store in shared preferences.

    The app does not configure an iOS backup exclusion. Apple device backups can include app data under your device backup settings. Apple handles those backups under its own policies.

    Retention and deletion

    Unsaved drafts remain until you save or discard them. Saved entries and media remain in app storage until you delete them or the operating system removes the app data. Deleting an entry removes it from the active database and attempts to remove media that no other entry uses. Delete all entries also removes tags, drafts, and unreferenced media. It does not remove your profile name or app preferences.

    OpenLog does not promise secure overwriting of deleted database data. Exported backups, files that you share, and copies in system backups remain until you or the service that holds them deletes them. A failed export can leave a temporary archive in app cache.

    OpenLog does not set a retention period for PostHog data or website request logs. PostHog and GitHub control those periods through their service settings and policies. The owner must confirm the current periods before publication.

    Security

    The optional app lock uses the device's biometric or passcode prompt. OpenLog stores the lock setting, not biometric templates or the device passcode. The app lock does not encrypt the timeline database, drafts, media, or backup archives. OpenLog does not add an encryption layer for those files. Protection also depends on your device and operating system settings.

    Privacy requests

    Your privacy rights depend on where you live. Some laws give you rights to access, correct, delete, or restrict personal information. Email the contact below to ask about a request. OpenLog has no account and does not keep a server copy of your timeline. The owner must confirm how to find and delete PostHog records before publication.

GitHub Pages hosts the OpenLog website. The website stylesheet requests fonts from Google Fonts. GitHub and Google receive website and font requests with ordinary connection data. The native app does not use browser cookies. The website source contains no analytics script or cookie code. The repository does not show the hosting providers' log or cookie practices. Read the GitHub privacy statement and Google Privacy Policy.

The website links to external services. If you open one, that service handles your visit under its own privacy terms.

Permissions and notifications

OpenLog uses these device permissions and pickers:

  • Photo-library access when you choose images to attach.
  • Microphone access when you start a recording.
  • Foreground location access when you ask to add or refresh a place.
  • The system file picker when you choose an attachment or backup.

OpenLog asks for notification permission shortly after the timeline opens. If you allow it, the app creates local notifications for backup and import progress. A completion notice can show the entry count and backup file size. The device can show these notices on its lock screen, subject to your notification settings. The code does not register a remote push-notification token.

Backups and sharing

When you export a backup, OpenLog creates a compressed archive with your entries, tags, app settings, profile name, locations, attachment details, and media files. OpenLog does not encrypt this archive. The app first writes it to temporary storage, then saves it to a folder you choose or opens the system share sheet. A file provider or app that you choose can receive a copy. OpenLog does not receive the copy that you save outside the app.

When you share a photo or open an attachment in another app, that app can receive the selected file. The device file picker can also show files from cloud storage providers. Those providers handle the file under their own terms.

Android system backup is enabled. OpenLog's Android rules include shared-preference files and exclude the SQLite database, media, drafts, and SecureStore preferences. Android can copy included preferences to its configured backup or device-transfer service. The code does not identify every value that another library can store in shared preferences.

14:- **Entries and preferences:** SQLite stores entry text, dates, tags, location coordinates and labels, attachment references, the local profile name, and preferences. A full-text index stores entry text and location labels for local search. [Schema](../src/services/db/migrations/v1.ts#L4-L38), [entry storage](../src/services/db/entries.ts#L21-L42), [search index](../src/services/db/schema.ts#L72-L98), and [preference storage](../src/services/db/settings.ts#L14-L105).
16:- **Profile and app lock:** The optional profile name is stored in SQLite. The app stores only an app-lock flag in SecureStore. The OS handles biometric or passcode checks. [Profile storage](../src/services/db/settings.ts#L75-L105), [lock storage](../src/services/auth/appLockStore.ts#L30-L56), and [local authentication](../src/services/auth/auth.ts#L19-L41).
19:- **Analytics:** A build sends PostHog events only when it has a project token and is not in JavaScript development mode. The client uses the US endpoint, captures app lifecycle events, and enables JavaScript exception and unhandled-rejection capture. Interaction autocapture and session replay are off. [PostHog configuration](../src/config/posthog.ts#L1-L25), [screen tracking](../App.tsx#L103-L129), and [event calls](../src/screens/compose/Compose.tsx#L213-L224).
22:- **Backups and sharing:** A manual backup contains timeline rows, tags, preferences, locations, and referenced media. The app compresses the archive but does not encrypt it. 23:- **System backups:** Android Auto Backup is enabled. The rules include shared-preference files and exclude the database, media, drafts, and SecureStore preferences. [Android app declaration](../app.json#L27-L42), [backup rules](../plugins/withAndroidBackupRules.js#L8-L38), and [EAS app declaration](../app.json#L11-L25).

The app sends `location_used` and `has_location` events, but it does not send GPS coordinates or place labels as event fields. The SDK also exposes the request IP to PostHog. Its IP-based location estimate is not disabled in app configuration. I've noticed a key oversight in the policy. I’m wondering if "OpenLog server" refers only to the company-owned server while PostHog acts as a third-party provider with access to this data. This brings up potential regulatory concerns regarding how user data can be shared with third-party services like Google and GitHub. Also, there's no in-app control mentioned regarding consent mode, which needs clarity.

**Reviewing app policies**

Alright, I’m working through the data type for emails from Gmail contacts, noting retention and user rights. There's no contact form, and I'm pondering whether to update the policy regarding the random ID and anonymous usage. I’ll also review the documentation for clarity, making sure we understand everything in plain English. I see the geolocation policy mentions Apple's Core Location, but it should specify `CLGeocoder`. I also want to clarify the Android Geocoder API details.

**Assessing app data policies**

Alright, I’m confirming that Google Fonts sends data and that GitHub Pages collects ordinary data. The Gmail integration looks good, and for Android shared preferences, there's auto backup without naming Google unless confirmed. iOS backups might include app data too, and I’m noting local encryption with app lock features like biometric or passcode options. I see the policy on data retention and secure overwriting needs addressing. There seems to be a potential issue with the app lock policy regarding biometric templates and metrics from the LocalAuthentication API.

**Evaluating local app settings**

I’ve confirmed that local storage is operating correctly. The Android backup rules include shared preferences and exclude SecureStore preferences, which is accurate. App lock is set via local settings rather than remotely. There’s a potential requirement to clarify what data is collected, how long it's stored, and specifics on retention for app content. Also, I’m concerned about possible cookie issues with Google Fonts. The policy states no cookie code in the site source, but the service could still set or read cookies.

Create a pull request on GitHub.

Upon success, the URL of the created pull request will be printed.

When the current branch isn't fully pushed to a git remote, a prompt will ask where
to push the branch and offer an option to fork the base repository. Any fork created this
way will only have the default branch of the upstream repository. Use `--head` to
explicitly skip any forking or pushing behavior.

`--head` supports `<user>:<branch>` syntax to select a head repo owned by `<user>`.
Using an organization as the `<user>` is currently not supported.
For more information, see <https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/10093>

A prompt will also ask for the title and the body of the pull request. Use `--title` and
`--body` to skip this, or use `--fill` to autofill these values from git commits.
It's important to notice that if the `--title` and/or `--body` are also provided
alongside `--fill`, the values specified by `--title` and/or `--body` will
take precedence and overwrite any autofilled content.

The base branch for the created PR can be specified using the `--base` flag. If not provided,
the value of `gh-merge-base` git branch config will be used. If not configured, the repository's
default branch will be used. Run `git config branch.{current}.gh-merge-base {base}` to configure
the current branch to use the specified merge base.

Link an issue to the pull request by referencing the issue in the body of the pull
request. If the body text mentions `Fixes #123` or `Closes #123`, the referenced issue
will automatically get closed when the pull request gets merged.

Use `--attach` to upload an image or video. The attachment is appended to the
body. If the body references an attached file, such as `![alt](./login.png)`, that
reference is rewritten to point at the uploaded asset instead. Paths in a
`--body-file` are relative to its directory, falling back to the working directory.
You can attach up to 50 files per command.

Alt text for an image follows the path after `#`, as in
`--attach './login.png#The login error state'`. Without it the filename is used.
A reference already in the body keeps the alt text written there. Video renders
as a player and has no alt text, so it cannot be given any.

If some attachments upload and others fail, the pull request is still created with the
ones that succeeded. The command then exits with a non-zero status, but the new pull
request's URL is still printed to stdout.

By default, users with write access to the base repository can push new commits to the
head branch of the pull request. Disable this with `--no-maintainer-edit`.

Adding a pull request to projects requires authorization with the `project` scope.
To authorize, run `gh auth refresh -s project`.


USAGE
  gh pr create [flags]

ALIASES
  gh pr new

FLAGS
  -a, --assignee login       Assign people by their login. Use "@me" to self-assign.
      --attach file          Attach an image or video file, in '<file>#<image alt text>' format
  -B, --base branch          The branch into which you want your code merged
  -b, --body string          Body for the pull request
  -F, --body-file file       Read body text from file (use "-" to read from standard input)
  -d, --draft                Mark pull request as a draft
      --dry-run              Print details instead of creating the PR. May still push git changes.
  -e, --editor               Skip prompts and open the text editor to write the title and body in. The first line is the title and the remaining text is the body.
  -f, --fill                 Use commit info for title and body
      --fill-first           Use first commit info for title and body
      --fill-verbose         Use commits msg+body for description
  -H, --head branch          The branch that contains commits for your pull request (default [current branch])
  -l, --label name           Add labels by name
  -m, --milestone name       Add the pull request to a milestone by name
      --no-maintainer-edit   Disable maintainer's ability to modify pull request
  -p, --project title        Add the pull request to projects by title
      --recover string       Recover input from a failed run of create
  -r, --reviewer handle      Request reviews from people or teams by their handle
  -T, --template file        Template file to use as starting body text
  -t, --title string         Title for the pull request
  -w, --web                  Open the web browser to create a pull request

INHERITED FLAGS
      --help                     Show help for command
  -R, --repo [HOST/]OWNER/REPO   Select another repository using the [HOST/]OWNER/REPO format

EXAMPLES
  $ gh pr create --title "The bug is fixed" --body "Everything works again"
  $ gh pr create --reviewer monalisa,hubot  --reviewer myorg/team-name
  $ gh pr create --project "Roadmap"
  $ gh pr create --base develop --head monalisa:feature
  $ gh pr create --template "pull_request_template.md"
  $ gh pr create --attach './login.png#The login error state'
  $ gh pr create --attach ./before.png --attach ./after.png

# Privacy audit

**Audit date:** 13 November 2026  
**Status:** Static code review. The policy draft needs owner confirmation and legal review before publication.

## Scope and limits

I reviewed app source, configuration, database schemas, permissions, analytics, backup flows, public pages, legal text, and release workflows. I traced data that the app stores, sends, exports, shares, or deletes.

I did not inspect `.env`, remote EAS variables, PostHog project configuration, store privacy forms, vendor contracts, or hosting logs. I did not capture live network traffic or test the app on a device or emulator. This report is not a legal opinion.

## Completed

- Updated [`webpage/privacy-policy.html`](webpage/privacy-policy.html) with a data-flow policy draft.
- Added [`docs/privacy-audit.md`](docs/privacy-audit.md) with findings, recommendations, owner questions, and regulatory review notes.
- Kept application code unchanged. The policy is marked **Draft for legal review** because production analytics settings, data retention, operator details, age range, and target markets need confirmation.

Key findings include PostHog analytics without an in-app opt-out, possible personal data in error reports or launch URLs, location coordinates sent to the device geocoder, unencrypted manual backups, and incomplete disclosure of system backups and website font requests.

## Pull request

Opened **draft PR #17**, [Add privacy policy and audit report](https://github.com/rwitesh/openlog/pull/17). It is not merged or published.

- `pnpm test`: 82 passed
- `pnpm typecheck`: passed
- `pnpm exec biome check src scripts`: passed
- `git diff --check` and HTML parsing: passed
- No device or emulator test was performed. I did not inspect the production EAS environment or PostHog project settings.

Entire status showed enabled. The commit created its checkpoint automatically; I did not create one manually. The pre-existing deletion of `.codex/hooks.json` remains untouched and is not in the PR.

I'm looking at a CSV that shows the aggregate installed audience by country, but it only includes columns for select countries, not most. It seems this could help with understanding Google Play distribution, specifically in places like Pakistan, India, the US, and Brazil. However, the report isn't comprehensive since it doesn't list all active countries or establish markets served. The export provides only four country metrics, which limits insights. I think we could update the report to properly cite the data and clarify what we know.

**Reviewing CSV privacy**

I notice the CSV is in my Downloads folder and shouldn't be committed publicly. The user wants me to check it for information. I can clarify to the owner that the report lists Pakistan, India, the US, and Brazil, but it isn't complete. They mentioned avoiding speculation about whether it serves all countries. We can say the report shows an installed audience in the four listed countries but refrain from naming unsupported countries in public communications. This data may help assess jurisdictions without being definitive.

**Clarifying policy on country distribution**

The owner mentioned they’re unsure about country distribution, advising not to mention what we don’t know. To accurately reflect this in our current policy, we can state, “Availability and applicable laws depend on your location.” They provided a local CSV to check, which includes daily totals for Pakistan, India, the US, and Brazil, but it doesn’t list all countries. Since the user prefers we don’t mention uncertainty, we should only use this evidence for internal clarifications. It's worth considering whether to include the local CSV in the internal report.

content.text:
entire checkpoint delete — Delete a checkpoint locally and from checkpoint remotes
Delete one checkpoint from this repository and from every checkpoint remote
that holds it.

The full checkpoint ID is required; prefixes are not accepted. Deleting from a
remote cannot be undone. A checkpoint on the entire/checkpoints/v1 branch is
removed from the branch tip only: the branch's history still contains it.

With --local-only no remote is contacted, except on the git-branch backend:
there a local removal reaches the sync remote on the next git push, so that
remote is checked, and --local-only (or a selection that leaves it out) is
refused while it holds a copy or cannot be reached. With push_sessions
disabled the removal is not pushed, but re-enabling it later pushes it.

Other checkpoints of the same sessions are listed but not deleted. Each one
carries the session's full transcript, so the session stays visible on
entire.com while any of them remain.

Without --force the command asks for confirmation, and refuses when it cannot
prompt. --dry-run prints what would be deleted and changes nothing.

Examples:
  entire checkpoint delete <id> --dry-run
  entire checkpoint delete <id>
  entire checkpoint delete <id> --remote origin --force
  entire checkpoint delete <id> --local-only --force

When to use this:
Destructive and irreversible on the remote. Never run this unless the user
explicitly asks to delete that checkpoint; do not pass --force on your own.

Current repo: gh/rwitesh/openlog  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
      --dry-run              Print what would be deleted without changing anything
  -f, --force                Delete without asking for confirmation
      --json                 Output as JSON
      --local-only           Delete only the local copy; leave every remote untouched
      --remote stringArray   Limit remote deletion to this remote; the local copy is still deleted (repeatable; "checkpoint_remote" names the dedicated checkpoint remote)

Inherited flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

OpenLog / Terms

Terms and Conditions

Last updated: 12 September 2026

These terms apply when you use OpenLog to keep a timeline of text, media, and other content.

1. Using OpenLog

You may use OpenLog to create entries containing text, photos, voice recordings, locations, documents, and other attachments. These entries are stored on your device; the current app does not provide account sign-in or cloud sync.

2. Your content

Your entries and attachments belong to you. We do not claim ownership of them, and OpenLog does not upload or sync your local content to our servers. You are responsible for having the rights to any content you add.

3. Backups are your responsibility

OpenLog provides export and import tools, including a preview before restore. Keep copies of important backups in a safe place. We cannot recover local content lost through a damaged, lost, reset, or replaced device when no usable backup exists.

4. Use the app lawfully

Do not misuse, disrupt, resell, or attempt to reverse engineer OpenLog or any related infrastructure. Do not use the app to store or distribute content that violates applicable law or another person’s rights.

5. Availability and changes

OpenLog is provided “as is” and “as available” to the extent permitted by law. We work to make it dependable, but features, supported platforms, and third-party services may change. We cannot guarantee that a device, operating system, or selected backup file will always be available or error-free.

6. Liability

To the extent permitted by law, Rwitesh Bera is not responsible for indirect losses or loss of data, profits, or goodwill arising from your use of OpenLog. Nothing in these terms limits rights or remedies that cannot legally be limited.

7. Updates to these terms

We may revise these terms as OpenLog changes. For material changes, we will provide notice in the app or on the website where practical. The current version is published here with its revision date, and continuing to use the app after an update means you accept the revised terms.

8. Contact

Questions? Email Rwitesh Bera.

OpenLog / Privacy Policy

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 13 November 2026 · Draft for legal review

This policy describes how the OpenLog app and website handle information.

Review notice. The code does not show whether production analytics are active, how long PostHog keeps data, which legal entity operates OpenLog, or which age groups and countries OpenLog serves. Resolve the owner questions in the audit report before publication.

How OpenLog works

OpenLog does not require an account or provide cloud sync. It stores your timeline in app storage on your device. The app does not upload the full timeline to an OpenLog server. Some services receive limited information, as described below.

Information stored on your device

OpenLog stores information that you add or choose:

  • Entry text, dates and times, tags, and locations that you add.
  • Location coordinates and the place label returned by the device geocoder.
  • Photos and voice recordings stored as app files.
  • Other files you attach, plus their names, types, and sizes.
  • Your optional profile name and app preferences.
  • Unsaved drafts, which can include text, media, tags, dates, and locations.

OpenLog uses these data to create, search, and display entries, save drafts, and apply your preferences. Search runs in the local database. The app copies selected media into its local storage.

OpenLog does not remove metadata from every attachment. Some photos stay as original files. They can contain information such as capture time or location.

Analytics and error reports

Some non-development app builds send analytics to PostHog when the build includes the PostHog project token. The code does not show whether the production build includes that token. The app does not ask for analytics consent or provide an in-app control to turn analytics off.

Product events can record:

  • Screen names and app install, update, open, active, and background events.
  • Entry creation, update, or deletion, plus whether an entry has text or a location.
  • Counts of attached photos, recordings, and files.
  • Recording duration, backup entry count, and backup file size.
  • Location use, app-lock changes, and the notification permission choice.

These event fields do not include entry text, media files, attachment names, or exact location coordinates. The app sends a persistent installation ID that does not contain your name. PostHog can use this ID to link events from the same installation. The SDK stores the ID and pending events in app storage. The app does not set an expiry for the event queue. It does not add your profile name or email address to product-event fields.

The PostHog SDK also sends the app identifier, version, build, and environment. It sends device model and manufacturer, operating system and version, locale, time zone, and screen size. PostHog receives the network request IP address. The app leaves PostHog's IP-based location estimate on. PostHog can infer an approximate region from that address, subject to project configuration. Events go to PostHog's US endpoint. OpenLog uses these events for product analytics and error diagnosis.

An app-open event can include the launch URL supplied by the operating system. The SDK also captures unhandled JavaScript errors, rejected promises, and errors from an app error boundary. Error reports can include error messages and stack traces. The app redacts file paths from errors sent through its manual reporting helper. Automatic error reports do not use that helper. An error message or launch URL can contain personal information.

The app does not record session replay, capture taps automatically, or collect console logs. The code does not set a PostHog data-retention period. PostHog's privacy policy and project settings govern its handling and retention.

Location

OpenLog requests foreground location only when you ask to add or refresh a place. It sends the coordinates to the native geocoding service to get a place label. iOS uses Apple's Core Location geocoder. Android uses the Android Geocoder API. The code does not name a fixed downstream provider for Android. These services can receive your coordinates.

OpenLog saves the coordinates and returned place label in the draft or entry on your device. It does not track location in the background. Analytics record whether you used location, not the coordinates or place label.

Fonts and the website

If you select an optional font that is not cached, OpenLog downloads it from the jsDelivr CDN and stores it on your device. The request identifies the font file and sends ordinary network data, such as your IP address. It does not include entry content. The app keeps downloaded fonts until you remove them or the operating system removes app data.

GitHub Pages hosts the OpenLog website. The website stylesheet requests fonts from Google Fonts. GitHub and Google receive website and font requests with ordinary connection data. The native app does not use browser cookies. The website source contains no analytics script or cookie code. The repository does not show the hosting providers' log or cookie practices. Read the GitHub privacy statement and Google Privacy Policy.

The website links to external services. If you open one, that service handles your visit under its own privacy terms.

Permissions and notifications

OpenLog uses these device permissions and pickers:

  • Photo-library access when you choose images to attach.
  • Microphone access when you start a recording.
  • Foreground location access when you ask to add or refresh a place.
  • The system file picker when you choose an attachment or backup.

OpenLog asks for notification permission shortly after the timeline opens. If you allow it, the app creates local notifications for backup and import progress. A completion notice can show the entry count and backup file size. The device can show these notices on its lock screen, subject to your notification settings. The code does not register a remote push-notification token.

Backups and sharing

When you export a backup, OpenLog creates a compressed archive with your entries, tags, app settings, profile name, locations, attachment details, and media files. OpenLog does not encrypt this archive. The app first writes it to temporary storage, then saves it to a folder you choose or opens the system share sheet. A file provider or app that you choose can receive a copy. OpenLog does not receive the copy that you save outside the app.

When you share a photo or open an attachment in another app, that app can receive the selected file. The device file picker can also show files from cloud storage providers. Those providers handle the file under their own terms.

Android system backup is enabled. OpenLog's Android rules include shared-preference files and exclude the SQLite database, media, drafts, and SecureStore preferences. Android can copy included preferences to its configured backup or device-transfer service. The code does not identify every value that another library can store in shared preferences.

The app does not configure an iOS backup exclusion. Apple device backups can include app data under your device backup settings. Apple handles those backups under its own privacy policy.

Retention and deletion

Unsaved drafts remain until you save or discard them. Saved entries and media remain in app storage until you delete them or the operating system removes the app data. Deleting an entry removes it from the active database and attempts to remove media that no other entry uses. Delete all entries removes tags and drafts. The app tries to remove media that no remaining entry uses. It does not remove your profile name or app preferences.

OpenLog does not promise secure overwriting of deleted database data. Exported backups, files that you share, and copies in system backups remain until you or the service that holds them deletes them. A failed export can leave a temporary archive in app cache.

OpenLog does not set a retention period for PostHog data or website request logs. PostHog and GitHub control those periods through their service settings and policies. The owner must confirm the current periods before publication.

Security

The optional app lock uses the device's biometric or passcode prompt. OpenLog stores the lock setting, not biometric templates or the device passcode. The app lock does not encrypt the timeline database, drafts, media, or backup archives. OpenLog does not add an encryption layer for those files. Protection also depends on your device and operating system settings.

Privacy requests

Your privacy rights depend on where you live. Some laws give you rights to access, correct, delete, or restrict personal information. Email the contact below to ask about a request. OpenLog has no account and does not keep a server copy of your timeline. The owner must confirm how to find and delete PostHog records before publication.

Children and policy changes

The previously published policy said OpenLog is not directed to children under 13. The app does not ask for age or enforce an age limit. The owner must confirm the intended age range before publication.

This page shows the current policy date. The app code does not provide an in-app notice for policy changes. The owner must confirm how OpenLog will notify users of material changes.

Contact

The website lists Rwitesh Bera as the maker of OpenLog. For privacy questions, email rwiteshbera@gmail.com. If you email us, your address, message, and any files you attach reach that Gmail mailbox. OpenLog uses the message to answer your request. Google handles the email under its privacy policy. The owner must confirm mailbox retention before publication. The owner must also add the legal operator name and postal address before publication.

OpenLog · made by Rwitesh Bera
Changelog Privacy Policy Terms & Conditions

## Findings

### F1. High: Analytics disclosure does not match the full data flow

The version of `webpage/privacy-policy.html` on `main` called analytics anonymous and said it did not collect location. This draft replaces those claims. The PostHog SDK creates a persistent pseudonymous identifier and attaches app, device, operating-system, locale, time-zone, and screen details. The app sends `location_used` and `has_location` events, but it does not send GPS coordinates or place labels as event fields. The SDK also exposes the request IP to PostHog. The app does not turn off the IP-based location estimate in PostHog. [Current policy draft](../webpage/privacy-policy.html), [PostHog setup](../src/config/posthog.ts#L3-L23), [locked SDK version](../pnpm-lock.yaml#L2321-L2332), [location event](../src/services/location/useLocation.ts#L30-L40), and [entry events](../src/screens/compose/Compose.tsx#L213-L224).

The app has no analytics consent prompt or opt-out. The privacy screen contains app lock, backup, and storage controls only. The production token is not in the repository. EAS selects a remote `production` environment, so this review cannot confirm whether production analytics are active. [Privacy screen](../src/screens/settings/PrivacySettings.tsx#L389-L464), [EAS profile](../eas.json#L7-L25), [environment template](../.env.example#L1), and [development guide](../DEVELOPMENT.md#L15-L18).

### F2. High: Error reports and launch URLs are not fully scrubbed

The app enables capture of unhandled JavaScript errors and rejected promises. `PostHogErrorBoundary` also sends error details and a component stack. Manual reports replace file paths with `<path>`, but automatic reports do not use that helper. The PostHog lifecycle event can also include the app launch URL. No global filter or launch-URL scrubber appears in the app configuration. I found no confirmed content leak, but an exception message or URL can contain personal information. [PostHog setup](../src/config/posthog.ts#L11-L19), [error boundary](../App.tsx#L121-L129), [app scheme](../app.json#L5-L12), [locked SDK version](../pnpm-lock.yaml#L2321-L2332), and [manual error reporting](../src/shared/utils/devLog.ts#L11-L39).

### F3. High: Local storage, backups, and app lock need clearer limits

The app uses SQLite and app files without an application-level encryption layer. The app lock calls the device authentication prompt, but it does not encrypt entries or attachments. The source also notes that the operating system can take an app-switcher snapshot before the JavaScript cover appears. [Database](../src/services/db/database.ts#L1-L28), [app lock](../src/services/auth/useAppLock.ts#L22-L47), and [lock storage](../src/services/auth/appLockStore.ts#L30-L56).

The manual `.openlog` archive is not encrypted. A copy can remain in app cache if saving or sharing fails after export. Android system backup includes shared preferences, but the repository does not list every value that libraries can store there. iOS app data has no configured backup exclusion. The current policy did not explain these paths. [Export archive](../src/services/backup/export/index.ts#L125-L132), [export cleanup](../src/services/backup/export/index.ts#L320-L324), [share fallback](../src/screens/settings/PrivacySettings.tsx#L137-L171), and [backup rules](../plugins/withAndroidBackupRules.js#L12-L38).

### F4. Medium: Location, font, website, and contact requests need disclosure

A location action sends coordinates to the native geocoder. iOS uses Core Location. Android calls the Android Geocoder API, but the repository does not name its downstream provider. The policy did not describe this request. The existing review file already lists this gap as P3-5. [Location service](../src/services/location/location.ts#L63-L85) and [open review finding](./review-findings.md#L9-L17).

The app also requests optional fonts from jsDelivr. The website stylesheet requests Google Fonts, and GitHub Pages hosts the site. A person who emails the listed Gmail address sends their message and any attached files to that mailbox. The code does not define retention for website logs or email. [Font resolver](../src/services/fonts/resolver.ts#L16-L27), [site CSS](../webpage/style.css#L1), [Pages workflow](../.github/workflows/pages.yml#L17-L36), and [contact address](../webpage/index.html#L15-L21).

### F5. Medium: Permission timing and attachment metadata need review

The app requests notification permission shortly after the timeline opens, not when a person starts a backup. Local completion notifications can show entry counts and backup size. The iOS configuration declares photo-library write use, but the reviewed app code opens a share sheet and does not call a photo-library write API. The image path can keep the original file, so embedded metadata can remain. [Timeline prompt](../src/screens/timeline/Timeline.tsx#L17-L39), [notification content](../src/services/notifications/notifications.ts#L65-L94), [iOS permission string](../app.json#L14-L25), [image path](../src/services/media/images.ts#L11-L48), and [share action](../src/services/media/share.ts#L15-L32).

The attachment picker accepts any file type. It can open selected files in another app. The policy did not describe file-provider or share-target handling. [Document picker](../src/services/media/attachments.ts#L20-L68).

The privacy contact uses a Gmail address. The code does not define mailbox-provider retention or how the owner handles requests. [Contact address](../webpage/index.html#L15-L21).

### F6. Medium: Public claims are broader than the implementation

The README says content stays on the device and is never uploaded. The website says the app works offline. The About screen says everything stays on the device. The terms say local content is not uploaded or synced. These statements omit PostHog telemetry, geocoding, font requests, system backups, and user-selected sharing. The old policy also promised practical notice for material changes, but no in-app notice path appears in the app. [README](../README.md#L7-L15), [website](../webpage/index.html#L85-L102), [About screen](../src/screens/settings/AboutSettings.tsx#L79-L84), and [terms](../webpage/terms.html#L27-L38).

The product guide says analytics never include locations. The app sends location-use and location-presence events. These events do not contain exact coordinates, so the guide and event design need a shared definition of location data. [Product guide](../AGENTS.md#L13-L16), [location event](../src/services/location/useLocation.ts#L30-L40), and [entry event fields](../src/screens/compose/Compose.tsx#L213-L224).

### F7. Medium: Retention, rights, operator, age, and jurisdiction are unknown

The app sets no local content expiry and has no single control that clears entries, profile details, preferences, font files, and analytics state. Delete-all removes entries, tags, and drafts. It tries to remove unreferenced media, but leaves profile and app preferences. SQLite deletion does not promise secure erasure. PostHog retention, website log retention, and email retention are not defined in the repository. [Delete-all action](../src/modules/entry/store/EntryStore.ts#L139-L147), [privacy settings](../src/screens/settings/PrivacySettings.tsx#L375-L386), and [database setup](../src/services/db/schema.ts#L33-L50).

The previous policy said OpenLog is not directed to children under 13, but the app does not ask for age or enforce an age limit. The repository names Rwitesh Bera as maker but does not give a legal operator name, postal address, target countries, or privacy-request process. It also does not contain Google Play Data Safety or Apple App Privacy disclosures. [Policy draft](../webpage/privacy-policy.html), [public contact and terms](../webpage/terms.html#L63-L79), [Android release workflow](../.github/workflows/release-android.yml#L1-L20), and [iOS config](../app.json#L11-L25).

## Recommendations

1. Confirm the production PostHog token, data region, GeoIP behavior, retention, processor terms, subprocessors, and deletion process.
2. Add a user-facing analytics choice or confirm that analytics run by default. Update the policy and store disclosures to match.
3. Disable launch-URL capture unless the app needs it. Add a tested event scrubber for exception text, stack traces, paths, and query values.
4. Decide whether to add encryption for local content and backup archives. Protect app-switcher snapshots before the JavaScript cover appears, or document this limit. Document Android and iOS backups. Remove temporary export files on every exit path.
5. Confirm the Android geocoder provider. Keep location use explicit and document that the platform geocoder receives coordinates.
6. Remove the unused photo-library write permission or add and document the feature that needs it. Use the narrowest photo-picker access available. Remove photo metadata before storage or explain that it can remain.
7. Move the notification prompt to a backup action. Limit completion details that appear on lock screens.
8. Self-host website fonts or disclose Google Fonts requests. Document GitHub Pages and contact-mail retention.
9. Align the README, website, About screen, terms, and product guide with the confirmed data flows.
10. Define retention, deletion, and privacy-request steps. Confirm the legal operator, address, age range, user countries, supported platforms, and notice process before publication.

## Owner clarifications

1. Does the production EAS environment contain `EXPO_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN`? Which release builds send PostHog events?
2. What PostHog region, retention period, GeoIP configuration, data-processing terms, and subprocessor list apply? Who handles deletion requests?
3. Does the owner want automatic error and launch-URL capture? What legal basis and user choice apply to analytics and location requests in each market?
4. Who is the legal operator and data controller? What legal name, postal address, privacy contact, and email-retention period belong in the policy?
5. Which countries and age groups does OpenLog serve? Is the iOS configuration a released product, and is any web app available?
6. What data can Android shared preferences contain? Does the owner intend Android cloud backup and device transfer? Does the owner want iOS backups to include app data?
7. Which service resolves Android coordinates? What service terms and retention apply to coordinates sent by the platform geocoder?
8. Does any supported feature save photos directly to the photo library? What rules apply to attachment metadata and files selected from cloud providers?
9. What privacy-request process and notice process does the owner use? Does any business practice share or sell data beyond the flows in this repository?

## Regulatory review

The repository does not establish the country of the operator, user countries, age range, or business thresholds. This review cannot decide which laws apply. Counsel must assess the launch markets. Candidate laws include GDPR, UK GDPR, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of India, US state privacy laws, and COPPA. Counsel must assess COPPA if the service targets children or the owner knows a child under 13 uses it.

Use data minimization, purpose limits, retention limits, and privacy by design as review criteria. Use the NIST Privacy Framework for a follow-up privacy review and OWASP MASVS for mobile security review. Confirm Google Play Data Safety and Apple App Privacy disclosures against the final build. This code review does not establish compliance with any law or framework.

**Updating website fonts**

I’m thinking about how to simplify website fonts and align with privacy. Removing Google Fonts could reduce third-party disclosures, and self-hosting seems like a good idea. It looks like the user wants a more minimal style for legal pages and prefers system fonts over anything flashy. I might suggest relocating the Google font import to specific HTML files to avoid unnecessary loads. Ultimately, I could consider changing the font variables to use system fallbacks, but that would eliminate external requests.

**Simplifying font usage**

The user wants fewer details and less tracking, which suggests simplifying the website's CSS. While the current homepage uses DM Sans and DM Serif, removing the Google Fonts import would lead to a fallback to sans-serif and Georgia. I noted that the site would still function properly, even if the fonts would differ slightly. By just removing the `@import` line, I could minimize requests to Google Fonts without changing any CSS variables — which seems beneficial for privacy!

**Reviewing Google Fonts usage**

I see the homepage only loads Google Fonts through a CSS import in `webpage/style.css`, with no direct font links in the HTML. Removing that line would eliminate third-party requests for Google Fonts on the homepage. However, I noticed that `docs/services/db/migrations/overview.html` still includes Google Fonts, but since it's separate and not deployed through Pages, users probably won't access it. I could update the policy to state that the OpenLog website source no longer requests Google Fonts.

OpenLog Contact

OpenLog / Privacy Policy

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 13 November 2026

OpenLog is an open-source, non-commercial Android app maintained by Rwitesh Bera. This policy covers the app and public website.

How OpenLog stores your information

OpenLog does not require an account or provide cloud sync. It stores your timeline on your device. Entries, media, drafts, profile name, and preferences stay in app storage unless you choose to export or share them.

Information stored on your device includes:

  • Entry text, dates, tags, and locations that you add.
  • Photos, voice recordings, documents, and other files.
  • Your optional profile name, app preferences, and unsaved drafts.

OpenLog uses this information to show and search your timeline, save drafts, and apply your preferences. Some photos stay as original files and can contain metadata such as capture time or location.

Analytics and error reports

OpenLog uses PostHog for analytics and error reports in the Android app. Events record screen names, app use, entry actions, media counts, recording durations, backup counts and sizes, location use, app-lock changes, and notification choices. The app does not ask for analytics consent or provide an in-app control to turn analytics off.

PostHog receives an installation ID, app and device details, and the IP address of each request. The ID does not contain your name, but it lets PostHog link events from the same installation. The IP address can show an approximate region. This data is pseudonymous, not anonymous. PostHog processes analytics in the United States.

Regular usage events do not include entry text, photos, recordings, attachment names, or exact location coordinates. Error reports can include technical error details. An event can also include a link that opened the app. Do not put private information in an app link. The app does not record screen sessions or taps.

PostHog controls its data retention under its service settings. Read the PostHog privacy policy.

Location

When you choose to add or refresh a location, Android obtains your current or recent location and uses its geocoding service to return a place label. That service can receive your coordinates. OpenLog saves the coordinates and place label with your entry or draft. The app does not track your location in the background. Analytics record location use, not your coordinates.

Fonts and website

If you choose an optional font, OpenLog downloads it from the jsDelivr CDN. The request includes the font file and standard connection information, such as your IP address. It does not include entry content. The app keeps the font on your device until you remove it or remove the app.

GitHub Pages hosts the OpenLog website. The site requests fonts from Google Fonts. GitHub and Google receive normal website and font request information. The site source does not include analytics or cookie code. Read the GitHub privacy statement and Google Privacy Policy .

Permissions and notifications

  • OpenLog requests photo access when you choose an image.
  • It requests microphone access when you start a recording.
  • It requests foreground location when you choose to add or refresh a place.
  • The system file picker lets you choose attachments and backups.

OpenLog asks for notification permission shortly after the timeline opens. If you allow it, the app shows local backup and import updates. A completion notice can show an entry count and backup size. Your device settings control whether these notices appear on the lock screen. OpenLog does not send remote push notifications.

Backups and sharing

An exported backup contains your entries, tags, locations, profile name, preferences, attachment details, and media. OpenLog compresses the archive but does not encrypt it. You choose where to save or share it. The chosen folder, service, or app receives the copy.

Android system backup can copy some app preferences. OpenLog's backup rules exclude the timeline database, media, and drafts. System backup settings control whether the included preferences are copied. When you share a photo or open a file in another app, that app receives the selected file.

Retention and deletion

Saved entries and media stay on your device until you delete them or remove the app. Unsaved drafts stay until you save or discard them. Delete all entries removes entries, tags, and drafts. It also tries to remove media that no entry uses. This action does not remove your profile name or preferences.

Exported backups, shared files, and system backup copies remain until you or their storage provider deletes them. The app does not promise secure erasure of deleted database data.

Security

The optional app lock uses your device's biometric or passcode prompt. It does not encrypt entries, media, drafts, or backup files. Protection also depends on your device and its settings.

Children and privacy requests

OpenLog is not directed to children under 13.

Privacy rights depend on where you live. Contact us to ask about a privacy request. OpenLog has no account and keeps no central copy of your timeline.

Contact

OpenLog is maintained by Rwitesh Bera. For privacy questions, email rwiteshbera@gmail.com. If you email us, Google handles your message through Gmail. We use your message to reply.

Changes to this policy

We will update this page when our data practices change.

OpenLog · made by Rwitesh Bera

OpenLog Contact

OpenLog / Privacy Policy

Privacy Policy

Last updated: 13 November 2026

OpenLog is an open-source, non-commercial Android app maintained by Rwitesh Bera. This policy covers the app and public website.

Information stored on your device

OpenLog does not require an account or provide cloud sync. It stores your timeline on your device so you can create, search, and view entries. Stored information includes entry text, dates, tags, locations, photos, recordings, attachments, your optional profile name, app preferences, and unsaved drafts.

Some photos stay as original files. They can contain metadata such as capture time or location. OpenLog stores selected media in app storage.

Analytics and error reports

OpenLog uses PostHog for analytics and error reports in the Android app. Events record screen names, app activity, entry actions, media counts, recording duration, backup counts and size, location use, app-lock changes, and notification choices. The app does not ask for analytics consent or provide an in-app way to turn analytics off.

PostHog receives a generated installation ID, app and device details, and the IP address of each request. The ID does not contain your name, but it lets PostHog link events from the same installation. The IP address can indicate an approximate region. This data is pseudonymous, not anonymous. PostHog processes analytics in the United States.

Regular usage events do not contain entry text, photos, recordings, attachment names, or exact location coordinates. Error reports can contain technical details. An app-open event can include a link that opened the app. Do not put private information in an app link. OpenLog does not record screen video or taps. PostHog's retention period follows its service settings.

Read the PostHog privacy policy.

Location

When you choose to add or refresh a location, Android gets your current or recent location and uses its geocoding service to return a place label. That service can receive your coordinates. OpenLog saves the coordinates and place label with your entry or draft. The app does not track your location in the background. Analytics record location use, not your coordinates.

Fonts and website

If you choose an optional font, OpenLog downloads it from the jsDelivr CDN. The request includes the font file and standard connection information, such as your IP address. It does not include entry content. The app keeps the font on your device until you remove it or remove the app.

GitHub Pages hosts the OpenLog website. The site requests fonts from Google Fonts. GitHub and Google receive normal website and font request information. The site source does not include analytics or cookie code. Read the GitHub privacy statement and Google Privacy Policy.

Permissions and notifications

  • OpenLog requests photo access when you choose an image.
  • It requests microphone access when you start a recording.
  • It requests foreground location when you choose to add or refresh a place.
  • The system file picker lets you choose attachments and backups.

OpenLog asks for notification permission shortly after the timeline opens. If you allow it, the app shows local backup and import updates. A completion notice can show an entry count and backup size. Your device settings control whether these notices appear on the lock screen. OpenLog does not send remote push notifications.

Backups and sharing

An exported backup contains your entries, tags, locations, profile name, preferences, attachments, and media. OpenLog compresses the archive but does not encrypt it. You choose where to save or share it. The chosen folder, service, or app receives the copy.

Android system backup can copy some app preferences. OpenLog's backup rules exclude the timeline database, media, and drafts. System backup settings control whether included preferences are copied. When you share a photo or open a file in another app, that app receives the selected file.

Retention and deletion

Saved entries and media stay on your device until you delete them or remove the app. Unsaved drafts stay until you save or discard them. Delete all entries removes entries, tags, and drafts. It also tries to remove media that no remaining entry uses. It does not remove your profile name or preferences.

Exported backups, shared files, and system backup copies remain until you or their storage provider deletes them. The app does not promise secure erasure of deleted database data.

Security

The optional app lock uses your device's biometric or passcode prompt. It does not encrypt entries, media, drafts, or backup files. Protection also depends on your device and its settings.

Children and privacy requests

OpenLog is not directed to children under 13.

Privacy rights depend on where you live. Contact us to ask about a privacy request. OpenLog has no account and keeps no central copy of your timeline.

Contact and changes

OpenLog is maintained by Rwitesh Bera as an independent project. For privacy questions, email rwiteshbera@gmail.com. Google handles email through Gmail. We use your message to reply. We will update this page when our data practices change.

OpenLog · made by Rwitesh Bera

# Privacy audit

**Local working notes. Do not publish.**

**Audit date:** 13 November 2026

edits.oldText: I did not inspect `.env`, remote EAS variables, PostHog project configuration, store privacy forms, vendor contracts, or hosting logs. I did not capture live network traffic or test the app on a device or emulator. This report is not a legal opinion.
edits.newText:
I did not inspect `.env`, remote EAS variables, PostHog project configuration, store privacy forms, vendor contracts, or hosting logs. The owner confirms that the production EAS build includes the PostHog token. I did not capture live network traffic or test the app on a device or emulator. This report is not a legal opinion.

## Owner facts

The owner confirms that OpenLog is a solo-maintained, open-source, non-commercial Android app. No iOS or web app has launched. The owner says the Android app is available in most countries, with some exclusions, but did not give a complete territory list.

A local Google Play installed-audience CSV shows daily totals and selected country columns. It does not identify all available or excluded countries. Do not use it as a full distribution list.

edits.oldText: The app has no analytics consent prompt or opt-out. The privacy screen contains app lock, backup, and storage controls only. The production token is not in the repository. EAS selects a remote `production` environment, so this review cannot confirm whether production analytics are active.
edits.newText: The app has no analytics consent prompt or opt-out. The privacy screen contains app lock, backup, and storage controls only. The owner confirms the production token is set. Its value remains outside the repository.

edits.oldText: The app sends `location_used` and `has_location` events, but it does not send GPS coordinates or place labels as event fields. The SDK also exposes the request IP to PostHog. The app does not turn off the IP-based location estimate in PostHog.
edits.newText: The app sends `location_used` and `has_location` events, but it does not send GPS coordinates or place labels as event fields. The SDK also exposes the request IP to PostHog. The app does not turn off the IP-based location estimate in PostHog. The owner confirms PostHog stores analytics in the United States.

edits.oldText: The previous policy said OpenLog is not directed to children under 13, but the app does not ask for age or enforce an age limit. The repository names Rwitesh Bera as maker but does not give a legal operator name, postal address, target countries, or privacy-request process. It also does not contain Google Play Data Safety or Apple App Privacy disclosures.
edits.newText: The previous policy said OpenLog is not directed to children under 13, but the app does not ask for age or enforce an age limit. The owner identifies Rwitesh Bera as the individual maintainer and says no company is registered. The exact age range, full territory list, postal address, and privacy-request process remain unknown. The repository does not contain a Google Play Data Safety declaration.

edits.oldText:
1. Does the production EAS environment contain `EXPO_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_PROJECT_TOKEN`? Which release builds send PostHog events?
2. What PostHog region, retention period, GeoIP configuration, data-processing terms, and subprocessor list apply? Who handles deletion requests?
3. Does the owner want automatic error and launch-URL capture? What legal basis and user choice apply to analytics and location requests in each market?
4. Who is the legal operator and data controller? What legal name, postal address, privacy contact, and email-retention period belong in the policy?
5. Which countries and age groups does OpenLog serve? Is the iOS configuration a released product, and is any web app available?

**Reviewing website adjustments**

The user confirmed there's no web app, only a site for report distribution. I see that the audit report uses an outdated "current policy." The owner facts state that "OpenLog is a solo-maintained, open-source, non-commercial Android app," which is good. I also noted that the F1 token is active, but the EAS variable is outside the repo. Now, I’ll focus on modifying the CSS as the user requested, making it simpler and removing unnecessary features for privacy.

**Adjusting CSS for simplicity**

I've changed the `.legal` style and removed the callout, but the current CSS still imports Google Fonts, which goes against the user's request for simpler styling. They mentioned that Google shouldn't be a concern like PostHog US because no identifiable data is involved. To align with their aim for minimal tracking, I think we can replace the Google Fonts with system fonts like Georgia. This will reflect in all pages. I should check `git status` to ensure all changes have been properly committed.

**Reviewing CSS changes**

I need to check the current legal styles in style.css. It seems the initial commit didn’t include this file, and now Git status shows that a change might have been made to `.legal h1`. I’m wondering if the previous tool edit was effective in updating the CSS. In our earlier task, it said there were "Successfully replaced 2 block(s)," indicating some success. But now we’ve decided to remove the @import, which also impacted `.legal` and `.callout` styles.
